explanations.explanation: Light is it, friend. The writer says, "He wraps Himself in light as with a garment…" Most of us grab a jacket on the way out the door. The writer pictures God wearing light. That's how great He is.

Clouds do show up in this psalm, just not as clothing. The writer pictures God making the clouds His chariot, and that comes in the next verse. The garment itself is light. It's an easy mix-up when the sky gets this crowded with pictures, friend.

Fire is in the psalm too, but it isn't the garment. The writer says God makes flames of fire His servants, which comes a couple of verses later. The garment is light. I think fire is a fair guess when the writer keeps stacking up glowing things, friend.
True. The writer pictures God making the clouds His chariot. Right after that, he has God walking on the wings of the wind. Clouds and wind, the whole sky is part of the picture, friend.

This one is true, and the text says it plainly. The writer pictures God making the clouds His chariot. The very next picture has Him walking on the wings of the wind. Clouds, wind, the whole sky is part of how the writer shows His greatness.
Yes, baker. The writer says God makes the winds His messengers. Flames of fire are His servants too. Even the weather has a job in this psalm, and I can't get my timer to do its one job.

Shelter is a nice thought, but that isn't what the text says. The writer says God makes the winds His messengers. The word shelter never comes up in this verse. Winds in this psalm are sent, not hidden behind.

A crown would be a fancy picture, but the writer doesn't use it here. He says God makes the winds His messengers. The flames of fire in the same verse are His servants. Wind and fire both get jobs in this verse, friend, and neither one gets a hat.

Above the mountains is right. The writer says God covered the earth with the deep like a garment, and the waters stood above the mountains. Think about that for a second. Friend, I get nervous when the sink fills up past the rim.

Valleys would be a lot of water, but the text goes higher than that. The writer says the waters stood above the mountains. That means even the tallest ground was covered. Valleys are too low for that picture, friend.

Just over the shores is much smaller than what the writer pictures. He says the deep covered the earth like a garment, and the waters stood above the mountains. That's not a spill at the edges. It's the whole earth wrapped up, friend.
The text says the opposite. At God's rebuke the waters fled, and at the sound of His thunder they hurried away. They don't rise, they run. Friend, I'd run too.
False is right. The writer says, "At Your rebuke the waters fled…" They don't rise, they leave in a hurry. Then the mountains rise and the valleys sink to the place God assigned for them.

explanations.answer: So they never cover the earth again
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says God set a boundary they cannot cross, "…that they may never again cover the earth." The line is drawn, and the water stays behind it. I wish my dough would respect a line like that.

explanations.answer: So the ships can sail safely
explanations.explanation: Ships do show up later in the psalm, but that's not the reason given here. The writer says the boundary is so the waters never again cover the earth (Psalm 104:9). The ships come up when the writer looks at the sea. Keep the boundary and the ships in separate pockets, friend.

explanations.answer: So the fish stay in one place
explanations.explanation: Fish aren't in this verse at all. The writer gives one reason for the boundary: that the waters may never again cover the earth. Sea creatures come up later, when the writer talks about the sea being full of living things. Good guess for a verse about water, though.

True. God sends springs into the valleys, and they give drink to every beast of the field. The wild donkeys quench their thirst there too. Friend, the whole field gets a drink and nobody has to stand in line.
The text says this is true. The writer says the springs give drink to every beast of the field. He even names the wild donkeys as ones who quench their thirst. The springs don't skip anybody.
Livestock is right. The writer says God makes the grass grow for the livestock. Then he adds crops for people to cultivate. Animals get the grass, people get the crops, and God set up both.

Lions do get mentioned, but they're not the ones this verse names. The writer says God makes the grass grow for the livestock. The young lions come up later, roaring for their prey and seeking their food from God (Psalm 104:21). Lions get their own mention, friend.

Storks are in the psalm, just not in this verse. The writer says God makes the grass grow for the livestock. The stork makes her home in the cypresses a few verses later (Psalm 104:17). Different verse, friend.
The LORD planted them. The writer says the cedars of Lebanon are the ones "…that He planted…" The psalm credits God Himself, friend. That's a fine thing to hold onto.

Solomon, Israel's king, is tied to Lebanon's cedars in the story of building the temple (1 Kings 5:6-10). But this psalm gives the credit somewhere else. The writer says the cedars of Lebanon are the ones "…that He planted…" meaning the LORD. Great guess for a cedar question, baker.

Hiram, king of Tyre, is tied to Lebanon's cedars too, because he supplied cedar for Solomon's building (1 Kings 5:1, 10). But this psalm credits someone else. The writer says the cedars of Lebanon are the ones "…that He planted…" meaning the LORD. Cedars were on Hiram's mind, friend, but not in this verse.

explanations.answer: God gives each creature its place
explanations.explanation: That's the big picture, baker. Birds nest in the cedars, the stork has the cypresses, the wild goats have the high mountains, and the rock badgers have the cliffs. Everybody has a spot. I wish my kitchen drawers were this organized.

explanations.answer: Every creature must fight for space
explanations.explanation: Fighting isn't in these verses. Each creature has its own home: the birds in the cedars, the stork in the cypresses, the wild goats on the mountains, the badgers in the cliffs. The writer shows a place for each one, friend.

explanations.answer: People rule over the wild places
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that here. It says the high mountains are for the wild goats and the cliffs are a refuge for the rock badgers. Those are the places the writer names for those animals. People don't show up in these verses at all.

The text says something different. When God brings darkness and it becomes night, the beasts of the forest prowl. Night is when they get moving, not when they settle down. Friend, I'd stay in the bakery.

False is right. The writer says God brings darkness, and it becomes night, "…when all the beasts of the forest prowl." They don't settle down, they head out. The lions withdraw later, when the sun rises.
Dens is it. The writer says when the sun rises, the young lions withdraw and lie down in their dens. Night shift is over, and they head home. Even the lions get to go home when the work's done.

Pastures aren't what the writer names here. He says that when the sun rises, the young lions withdraw and lie down in their dens. The grass in this psalm is for the livestock (Psalm 104:14). Dens is the word for the lions, friend.

Valleys are in the psalm, where the springs flow (Psalm 104:10), but this verse names something else. The writer says the young lions lie down in their dens when the sun rises. Dens is the word he uses. I think valleys is a fair guess, since the earlier verses were so full of them.
Wisdom, baker. The writer says, "In wisdom You have made them all…" Every creature, from the smallest to the biggest, was made with wisdom. Nothing was thrown together.

Thunder does show up in this psalm, but not here. The writer says the waters hurried away at the sound of God's thunder (Psalm 104:7). For the creatures, the writer says God made them all in wisdom. Big sound, different verse, friend.
Silence isn't in this verse. The writer says, "In wisdom You have made them all…" With lions roaring and birds singing in this psalm, silence would be a stretch. Wisdom is the answer, friend.
Frolic is right. The writer says God formed Leviathan to frolic in the sea. That's the writer's picture of it, friend. Leviathan is out there playing.
Hunting isn't what the writer says here. He says God formed Leviathan to frolic there. Hunting was the lions' business, roaring for their prey at night (Psalm 104:21). Leviathan gets the play part.

Sleeping isn't what the writer says here. He says God formed Leviathan to frolic in the sea. The ones who lie down are the young lions, in their dens when the sun rises (Psalm 104:22). Leviathan is out playing, friend.

Food is right. The writer says all creatures look to God to give them their food in due season. Every one of them is waiting on Him. When God opens His hand, they're satisfied with good things (Psalm 104:28).

Names aren't what the creatures look to God for in this verse. The writer says they look to Him to give them their food in due season. That's what they're waiting on. Good thought, but the verse is about dinner.

Strength is a nice thing to ask for, but the verse says something else. The writer says all creatures look to God to give them their food in due season. That's what they're waiting on. Friend, I'd want snacks first too.

explanations.answer: They die and return to dust
explanations.explanation: That's what the verse says, and it's a heavy one. When God hides His face, they're terrified. When He takes away their breath, they die and return to dust. The very next verse turns toward life: when He sends His Spirit, they are created.

explanations.answer: They fall into a deep sleep
explanations.explanation: The writer is plainer than that. He says that when God takes away their breath, they die and return to dust. It's a heavy verse, friend. Sleep isn't what it says.

explanations.answer: They wander off to the sea
explanations.explanation: The sea is in this psalm, but not in this verse. The writer says that when God takes away their breath, they die and return to dust. It's a heavy verse, baker. The next verse turns toward life: when He sends His Spirit, they are created.

Created is it. The writer says, "When You send Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth." New life, and the whole earth made new. I know a thing or two about being renewed, friend.
Scattered isn't in this verse. The writer says that when God sends His Spirit, they are created. And He renews the face of the earth. Nothing is blown apart here, friend.

Silenced isn't in this verse. The writer says that when God sends His Spirit, they are created, and He renews the face of the earth. It's a verse about new life starting up. Created is the word he uses, baker.
They smolder, friend. The writer says, "He touches the mountains, and they smolder." Just a touch, and mountains smoke. That's how powerful the writer says He is.
Bowing isn't what the writer says. He says that when God touches the mountains, they smolder. The earth trembles when He looks at it. Smoke is the picture here, friend.
Splitting isn't in the verse. The writer says that when God touches the mountains, they smolder. The earth trembles at His look. That's a powerful picture without any splitting, baker.
True. The writer says, "I will sing to the LORD all my life…" He adds that he will sing praise to his God while he has his being. That's a long set list, friend.

This one is true, and the writer says it himself. He says, "I will sing to the LORD all my life; I will sing praise to my God while I have my being." It's a promise that lasts as long as he does. He's in it for the whole show.
That's his reason, friend. The writer says, "May my meditation be pleasing to Him, for I rejoice in the LORD." He doesn't bring up a record or a résumé. He just says he's glad in the LORD.

The writer doesn't give that as his reason. He hopes his meditation will be pleasing to the LORD, and he says why: he rejoices in the LORD. Nothing about a perfect record shows up in this verse. It's joy that he points to, baker.
The writer doesn't say that here. His reason is that he rejoices in the LORD. It's a verse full of gladness, friend. Fear of anger isn't in it.
